output.title: Mend & Move Refill Co.
output.narrative:
Mend & Move Refill Co. is a privately owned business based in Birmingham. It sells concentrated household-cleaning products in reusable aluminium bottles. Customers buy starter bottles and then order refill sachets through the company’s website or app. The business states that its purpose is to make lower-waste cleaning products convenient and affordable for busy households.

The business has grown as more customers use online subscriptions and seek products with less single-use plastic. However, customer interviews suggest that some potential customers still see refills as less convenient than buying established brands in supermarkets. Mend & Move’s main customer group is households aged 25–44, particularly customers who value home delivery and can manage subscriptions through a mobile phone.

For the year ended 31 March 2026, Mend & Move generated revenue of £1.80m and made a profit of £150,000. It holds £85,000 cash at the year end. Managers explain that cash has been reduced by buying refill sachets in advance from suppliers and by paying for new delivery crates. The owners have set objectives to increase revenue, protect profit per order and maintain enough cash to pay suppliers on time. They disagree about which objective should receive greatest priority during the next year.

Mend & Move operates in a UK market for household-cleaning refill subscriptions. Its marketing manager has proposed a £240,000 investment in an automated packing and demand-forecasting system. The system would use customer-order data to predict subscription demand, reduce picking errors and send personalised refill reminders through the app. It could enable faster dispatch and reduce packaging waste, but staff would need training and some warehouse roles could change. The investment would be paid from cash and a bank loan.

Supporters argue that the system could help Mend & Move respond to customers’ growing use of online shopping, improve convenience and reduce wasted stock. Critics are concerned that inaccurate customer data, system failures or poor app recommendations could damage trust. They also argue that the business should first improve its cash position and test whether customers will respond positively to more personalised digital communication.

output.title: ParcelPedal Ltd: Positioning, international growth and FlexLoad innovation
output.narrative:
This Revision-authored stimulus concerns ParcelPedal Ltd, a Bristol-based manufacturer of electrically assisted cargo trikes for urban delivery fleets. Its 85 employees assemble trikes in the UK and provide fleet customers with repair training, replacement parts and a 48-hour technical-support service. ParcelPedal targets a narrow market of delivery firms that need reliable vehicles with low downtime, rather than selling to individual cyclists.

ParcelPedal’s current trike is designed so that mechanics can replace damaged panels, brakes and battery mounts without replacing the whole vehicle. This repairability, together with its support service, is central to the firm’s marketing. However, RideFast imports standardised cargo trikes at a lower price, while UrbanHaul sells UK-assembled trikes with more conventional designs. ParcelPedal has capacity to assemble 1,400 trikes annually; it sold 1,200 in 2024.

A Dutch distributor has asked ParcelPedal to supply 500 trikes in 2026 for delivery fleets in several cities. The distributor would handle customer sales, but ParcelPedal would remain responsible for supplying parts. Dutch fleet managers have requested removable batteries and narrower cargo modules for use in constrained urban spaces. Exporting from Bristol would add £220 transport and administration cost per trike. Alternatively, ParcelPedal could form a joint venture with a Dutch maintenance business. This would require a £450,000 initial equity investment, would give the business local repair capability, and could avoid the £220 export cost. The Dutch partner wants influence over product adaptations and local marketing.

The board is also considering FlexLoad, a proposed product and process innovation. FlexLoad would have removable batteries and interchangeable cargo modules, helping it meet the Dutch requests and allowing UK customers to choose different modules for parcels, groceries or medical supplies. Development and tooling would cost £2.00m, and staff training would cost a further £150,000. ParcelPedal has £1.10m available cash for the project and would need bank finance for the remainder. A patent application has been submitted for the modular mounting system, but the patent has not yet been granted.

FlexLoad would use an automated frame-welding and testing cell. Management forecasts that this would reduce direct production cost by £240 per FlexLoad trike, increase annual capacity to 1,600 trikes and reduce the proportion of trikes requiring warranty repairs in their first year from 7% to 3%. Four existing fleet customers have trialled prototypes, but the sales forecast remains dependent on customers accepting the higher price. The new removable battery would be supplied by one specialist supplier, creating a new dependency. The board must decide whether to proceed with FlexLoad, retain the current model, or prioritise international expansion using the existing design.

LoopFill Ltd is a privately owned business in Leeds that fills reusable household-cleaning liquids into pouches for independent retailers and regional supermarkets. Its largest customer has asked LoopFill to supply an additional 50,000 pouches during the next financial year, provided the business can meet agreed delivery dates.

The directors are considering an automated filling and packing line costing £200,000. They expect it to reduce bottlenecks on the evening shift, but staff will need training before it is used. The business has £95,000 cash at the end of 2025, although its directors want to retain at least £80,000 as a cash buffer because customers normally pay 45 days after delivery.

Management has linked rising staff departures to the difficulty of covering evening shifts, but exit interviews have also mentioned pay and training. The operations manager has warned that faster filling must not increase pouch leaks or customer complaints.

To fund the line, LoopFill has received a bank-loan offer and has also been approached about an equity crowdfunding campaign. Its finance manager has suggested factoring some customer receivables to improve day-to-day cash flow. The directors must decide how to finance growth while protecting control, cash flow and service quality.

output.title: Northstar Home Systems: scaling a connected heating-controls range
output.narrative:
Northstar Home Systems Ltd is a Leeds-based manufacturer and online seller of smart heating controls for UK households. It employs 186 people and generated revenue of £8.4m in the year ended March 2026. Its main product, the Halo thermostat, is assembled in Leeds from imported circuit boards, UK-made casings and bought-in sensors. Northstar’s objective is to grow Halo sales while protecting product reliability and avoiding further pressure on cash.

Demand for Halo has increased after large energy retailers began listing it online. Forecast sales for the next 12 months are 52,000 units, compared with 39,000 units in the previous year. However, the forecast assumes that retailers’ promotions continue and that competing low-priced products do not reduce Northstar’s selling price. The operations director believes the existing packing line will not reliably handle peak weekly demand. The board is considering an automated packing line, which would also provide serial-number scanning for traceability and reduce manual packing errors.

Northstar currently has a five-layer functional hierarchy. Production, purchasing, sales and finance managers report to the operations director, who refers significant decisions to the managing director. Most production staff have permanent full-time contracts and work to detailed procedures. Managers say this structure has helped quality control, but team leaders report slow decisions when shortages occur. The proposed change would remove one management layer, create multi-skilled production cells and give cell leaders authority to alter daily staffing and production schedules within agreed quality and spending limits. Some supervisors fear redundancy or loss of status; some assemblers are concerned about learning new tasks and being measured through the new scanning system. The managing director has announced the intended launch date but has not yet decided whether to use a pilot, consultation meetings, training, or a faster compulsory implementation.

Northstar’s March management accounts showed an operating profit of £504,000, but its closing cash balance was only £96,000. Customers, including retailers, usually pay 60 days after delivery, while Northstar pays its main circuit-board supplier 30 days after invoice. Inventory has risen from £610,000 to £1.05m as purchasing staff ordered larger batches to avoid shortages. The finance director’s rolling forecast shows a possible cash shortfall in July if £420,000 of retailer receipts arrive two weeks late. Management is considering tighter customer-credit control, selling surplus slow-moving casings, negotiating longer supplier terms, reducing buffer stock, delaying the packing-line purchase or using an overdraft. Each option could affect customer relationships, supplier reliability, output or future growth.

The circuit boards currently come from one supplier in Malaysia. Its unit price is £18.40 and its normal lead time is 10 weeks; it requires minimum orders of 12,000 boards. A UK supplier has offered boards at £20.10 each, in batches of 3,000, with a three-week lead time. The UK supplier has spare capacity but has supplied Northstar only on a small trial order. A recent port delay added three weeks to a Malaysian delivery, causing Northstar to use almost all of its buffer inventory. A missed delivery of Halo thermostats would expose Northstar to retailer penalties and may damage online customer ratings. The purchasing manager argues that the Malaysian supplier remains cheaper; the sales director argues that lower inventory, shorter lead times and dual sourcing could be worth the higher purchase price.

To decide how to secure circuit-board supply for the coming winter peak, Northstar has estimated outcomes using internal data. If it continues with the Malaysian supplier alone, managers estimate a 0.70 probability of normal supply, producing an expected seasonal contribution of £780,000, and a 0.30 probability of a serious delay, producing a contribution of £270,000 after lost sales and expedited freight. Establishing a dual-source arrangement would cost £95,000 in testing, supplier onboarding and revised quality checks. Under dual sourcing, management estimates a 0.85 probability of normal supply with seasonal contribution before these costs of £745,000, and a 0.15 probability of a serious delay with contribution before these costs of £510,000. The estimates are based on Northstar’s experience and supplier discussions rather than independently verified probabilities.

The engineering contractor has offered to shorten activity E by two weeks for an additional £36,000, but this would require weekend access to the factory. The operations director also wants to know whether the project schedule alone is sufficient, since the same maintenance technicians are needed for normal production and for installing the line.

Final inspection may still be useful to catch unexpected faults, but quality assurance is more likely to address the process causes of Harbour Homeware's repeated defects.

Shows thorough, well-applied analysis of the financing and ownership implications for Northton. Develops linked consequences of public equity finance against debt, including dilution/control and governance or accountability effects. Clearly recognises that Northton is already an Ltd, so its shareholders normally already have limited liability; becoming a plc does not newly create this protection. Distinguishes shareholder liability from directors' responsibilities.

indicative_content: Northton is already a limited company, so its shareholders normally already benefit from limited liability. Conversion to a plc would not newly limit the founders' normal shareholder exposure.

A plc can offer shares to the public, potentially allowing Northton to raise a larger amount of share capital for the production site than may be available from the founders or a small private investor group.

Issuing new shares provides equity capital without contractual interest payments or scheduled loan repayments. This could reduce fixed cash-flow pressure while the new site is being built and before it generates sufficient sales.
Equity investors acquire ownership interests. If public investors buy newly issued shares, the founders' percentage ownership is diluted, potentially weakening their ability to control decisions.

More shareholders and a wider separation between ownership and management can increase the need for clear reporting, oversight and accountability. Investors may expect information and returns, including possible dividends, although dividends are not guaranteed.

A large long-term loan would avoid ownership dilution and allow the founders to retain control, but interest and repayment obligations would create fixed demands on future cash flows and increase financial risk if expansion income is uncertain.
The directors would still have responsibilities for governing the company and making decisions appropriately. Limited liability for shareholders does not remove directors' duties.
A plc may face greater shareholder scrutiny and possible pressure over performance or share price. This may constrain the founders' freedom compared with the current closely held Ltd structure.

A supported conclusion may depend on whether Northton's priority is protecting cash flow during uncertain expansion or retaining close founder control, and on the availability and terms of debt versus equity finance.
mark_scheme.model_answer:
Becoming a plc could enable Northton to issue shares to a much wider group of investors and raise substantial share capital for the new site. Unlike a large loan, this equity finance would not require contractual interest payments or repayments. This could be valuable while the site is being built, because Northton may have high cash outflows before the expansion produces additional revenue.

However, investors buying newly issued shares would gain ownership interests, so the founders' proportion of the company would fall. Their control over major decisions could therefore weaken. A plc also has a wider shareholder base, increasing the need for reporting, oversight and accountability. Shareholders may expect returns, potentially including dividends, although a dividend is not guaranteed.

Northton is already an Ltd, so its shareholders normally already have limited liability. Becoming a plc would not newly provide this protection; the main change is greater access to public equity finance alongside more diluted ownership and shareholder scrutiny. Limited liability also does not remove the founders' responsibilities as directors. If Northton's future cash flows are uncertain, avoiding fixed loan repayments may justify dilution; if retaining founder control is the priority, a loan may be preferred despite its repayment risk.

Northshore Home Systems makes smart heating controls. It plans to launch a new product range within 18 months and needs more software technicians, field installers and customer-support employees across two UK locations. Management is concerned that several experienced technicians have left, while applicants have varied backgrounds and expectations about flexible working. The business wants to improve employee engagement, build a pipeline of talent, provide training for new technology, increase workforce diversity and ensure employees act consistently with its customer-care values. 

The operations director favours a hard HRM approach: set precise staffing numbers, tightly measure individual output, use fixed procedures and keep labour costs low. The people director favours a soft HRM approach: consult employees on job design, offer development and career opportunities, use flexible working where possible, and involve employee representatives in major changes. Managers also report that some service delays may result from unclear workflows and unsuitable software, rather than solely from employee effort.
output.stem: Evaluate whether Northshore Home Systems should adopt a predominantly soft HRM approach, rather than a predominantly hard HRM approach, to achieve its human resource objectives.

levels.descriptor: Shows limited relevant knowledge of HRM, perhaps identifying one hard or soft HRM feature. Application to Northshore is generic or asserted. Analysis is limited, with little or no supported judgement.

Shows some accurate knowledge of hard and/or soft HRM and makes some relevant use of the context. Explains one or more plausible effects on employees or business performance, although chains of reasoning may be partial. A judgement is present but limited or insufficiently justified.

Shows sound, reasonably broad knowledge of HR objectives and hard and soft HRM. Applies this to Northshore's skills, retention, technology or workforce issues. Analyses developed consequences for capability, engagement, cost, service or flexibility. Reaches a supported judgement, though evaluation may be uneven or alternatives may not be fully weighed.

Shows detailed and well-selected knowledge of the relevant HR objectives and approaches. Application is consistently linked to Northshore's planned launch, workforce needs and operational constraints. Analysis develops several connected effects and recognises that employee performance also depends on job design, systems and resources. Evaluation compares the approaches and reaches a well-supported, context-sensitive judgement.

Shows precise, comprehensive and selective knowledge, integrated throughout a sustained response. Analysis rigorously examines how a blended or predominantly soft approach could affect workforce capability, engagement, retention, values, diversity and service, alongside costs, control and implementation risks. Evaluation is balanced and perceptive, tests assumptions in the case, and reaches a clear, prioritised judgement with convincing conditions and trade-offs.

indicative_content: Hard HRM focuses on aligning workforce numbers, costs, performance and deployment with business requirements. It is not simply harsh management. For Northshore, it could help ensure enough installers, technicians and support employees are available in the required locations before the product launch.

Soft HRM treats employees as a source of capability and commitment, using involvement, communication, development and trust to support organisational outcomes. It is not automatically better for employees or incompatible with business targets.

A predominantly soft approach could support engagement and retention among experienced technicians. Consultation over job design and flexible working may increase perceived autonomy or work-life fit, reducing the loss of valuable product and customer knowledge. This could improve continuity and service quality during the launch.

Training and wider development are important because Northshore's new product creates a technology-related capability requirement. Development may enable existing employees to move into new roles and support succession, potentially reducing recruitment uncertainty. However, training attendance does not prove improved performance; new skills must be used in supportive workflows, with suitable systems and management support.

Talent acquisition should begin with the capabilities required, rather than automatically replacing former job descriptions. Northshore may need a longer-term pipeline for scarce software technicians, while internal progression can retain organisational knowledge. External recruitment may still be required to bring skills or experience not held internally.

An inclusive approach to recruitment, development and employee voice could help Northshore access a wider range of applicants and perspectives. However, diversity benefits depend on inclusive practice, communication and fair implementation, rather than merely increasing the number of applicants from different backgrounds.

Soft HRM can reinforce customer-care values if leaders, rewards, job design and everyday decisions consistently support those values. Employee involvement may identify delivery risks or customer problems earlier. A stated value will have little effect if output measures or manager behaviour reward speed at the expense of customer care.

The operations director's hard approach may be valuable where launch timing, staffing coverage, cost control and consistent procedures are critical. Clear workforce planning is needed to match the number, skills, locations and timing of employees to expected demand. Flexible arrangements cannot remove the need for dependable service cover and coordination.

Tight individual output targets may create focus and expose capacity problems, but can encourage unintended behaviour if they reward speed over quality or collaboration. They may also undermine the customer-care values that Northshore seeks to embed.

The reported service delays indicate that low effort may not be the root cause. If workflows or software are unsuitable, pressure, targets or motivational initiatives alone will not solve the problem. Northshore should diagnose process, resources, capability and job-design issues before attributing delays to employee motivation.

Employee representatives can provide structured consultation over major changes and may improve information quality and trust. However, consultation can slow decisions and will only be meaningful if management considers and responds to concerns. It does not necessarily transfer final decision authority.

A balanced conclusion may favour predominantly soft HRM for scarce skills, retention, technology-related development and values alignment, but retain hard HRM disciplines for workforce planning, clear performance expectations, cost control and service coverage. The appropriate balance depends on labour-market scarcity, financial capacity, whether systems are fixed, and the time available before launch.
mark_scheme.model_answer:
Northshore should use predominantly soft HRM, but only if it retains hard HRM controls over the workforce requirements needed for the launch. A soft approach would be particularly suitable because the business needs scarce software technicians and is losing experienced employees. Development, career opportunities and employee involvement could make employees more likely to remain, while training could build the capability needed for the new smart-heating range. Retaining technicians also preserves product and customer knowledge, which could improve service during a period of change.

Soft HRM could also support Northshore's customer-care values. If employees are consulted about job design and service problems, they may identify barriers that senior managers cannot see. This is important because delays may be caused by unclear workflows and unsuitable software rather than low effort. In this situation, tighter output targets might increase pressure without fixing the cause. In addition, involving employees and using inclusive recruitment and development may help Northshore attract a wider talent pool and improve engagement.

However, a soft approach alone would be insufficient. Northshore must still plan the required number of installers, technicians and support staff by location and timing. The launch could fail if flexible working or lengthy consultation leaves shifts uncovered or slows decisions. Clear procedures and performance expectations may also be necessary for consistent installation and customer support. Furthermore, training will only improve performance if employees can apply new skills through effective software, workflows and management support.

Therefore, Northshore should adopt a predominantly soft approach because retention, capability development, employee voice and values alignment are central to its current problems. Nevertheless, it should combine this with hard HRM measures such as workforce planning, clear service standards and cost monitoring. The balance should be reviewed as the launch approaches: where skills are scarce and service quality depends on expertise, soft practices deserve priority; where coverage, safety or launch deadlines are at risk, firmer workforce controls are justified.

Harbour Homeware makes three ranges of reusable drinks bottles. Demand for its standard range is high and relatively predictable, but demand for its premium personalised range changes frequently. The business currently uses batch production. Products move between separate cutting, printing and assembly areas, and the printing area often creates queues. Managers report that employees spend time moving stock between areas and that some batches require rework because printed designs are incorrect.

The operations director proposes investing in automated printing and assembly equipment arranged in a product layout for the standard range. This would create a more capital-intensive flow process. The director also wants to introduce a lean programme: employees would suggest small improvements, batch sizes would be reduced and raw-material inventory would be delivered closer to when it is needed. The proposal would reduce storage space and could release cash currently tied up in stock.

However, the equipment would require substantial initial investment, specialist maintenance and employee retraining. Harbour Homeware has had several late deliveries from one key supplier. The sales director is concerned that lower inventory could lead to stock-outs, while the production manager argues that some spare capacity is needed to deal with demand peaks and equipment downtime.
output.stem: Evaluate whether Harbour Homeware should implement the operations director’s proposal to improve efficiency and productivity. In your answer, consider the proposed process and technology, capacity and the bottleneck, lean operations and inventory management.

levels.descriptor: Shows limited relevant knowledge of operations concepts. Application to Harbour Homeware is weak or absent. Assertions about the proposal are largely unsupported, with little analysis or judgement.

Shows some relevant knowledge and some application to Harbour Homeware. Includes one or more developed but partial chains of analysis, such as linking automation or lower inventory to cost or service. Evaluation is limited, generic or unsupported.

Shows sound knowledge of several relevant operations concepts and applies them to the business. Analyses benefits and drawbacks of the proposed process, technology, lean approach or inventory changes. Makes a judgement, although it may not fully weigh the most important contextual conditions.

Shows thorough and accurate knowledge, consistently applied to Harbour Homeware. Develops clear, linked analysis of capacity/bottleneck issues, process and technology choices, lean improvement and inventory trade-offs. Evaluation is balanced and reaches a supported judgement that recognises relevant conditions and risks.

Shows precise, well-selected and fully integrated knowledge of operations management. Sustained analysis explains how the proposal could affect efficiency, productivity, quality, capacity, cash and customer service across the system. Evaluation is perceptive and context-led, weighing implementation and resilience risks against likely gains. Reaches a clear, well-justified judgement, potentially recommending a staged or differentiated implementation.

indicative_content: Efficiency concerns the economic conversion of resources into required outcomes; productivity is output per unit of input. Greater total output alone would not prove higher productivity, particularly if defects and rework rise.

The existing printing area is a likely bottleneck because queues form there. Improving this constrained stage may raise total throughput, whereas improving a non-bottleneck stage may not increase overall output.

For the predictable, high-volume standard range, automated printing and assembly in a product layout could reduce movement and waiting between separate areas. Standardisation may improve consistency, permit a flow process and lower labour input per good unit, improving productivity and potentially unit costs.

Automation is a technology choice rather than proof that the whole operation is necessarily a flow process. Its benefits depend on suitable volume, stable demand, reliable maintenance, staff capability and effective process design.

The capital-intensive equipment requires high initial expenditure, specialist maintenance and retraining. If demand for the standard range falls, or downtime occurs, fixed costs may be spread over fewer units. The investment could therefore reduce flexibility and place pressure on cash.

The premium personalised range has changing demand and greater variety. Retaining a more flexible batch or labour-intensive process for this range may be more suitable than forcing all products through a standardised flow line.

Lean operations can remove avoidable waste, including unnecessary movement, waiting, defects and excess inventory. Employee-led continuous improvement can use staff knowledge to identify causes of printing errors and test improvements before standardising successful changes.

Lean should not simply mean cutting staff, maintenance or every buffer. Reducing batch size before improving setup or process reliability could create additional downtime; removing necessary maintenance could increase breakdowns.
Deliveries closer to need can reduce raw-material inventory, storage costs and working capital tied up in stock. This may release cash and expose underlying process problems.

Lower inventory increases dependence on reliable suppliers and accurate information. Harbour Homeware's record of late delivery makes stock-outs and interrupted production more likely, potentially losing sales and damaging service.

Some spare capacity can protect customer service during demand peaks and provide time for maintenance. Very high utilisation is not automatically efficient if it produces queues, delays, quality problems or a lack of resilience.

A supported conclusion may recommend a phased trial on the stable standard range, first relieving and monitoring the printing bottleneck, training employees and retaining an appropriate buffer stock or contingency supplier arrangement. Full implementation is more justified only if expected demand, supplier reliability and maintenance capability support it.
mark_scheme.model_answer:
Harbour Homeware should implement parts of the proposal, but a full and immediate switch would be risky. The strongest case is for redesigning the standard range first, while keeping more flexibility and some inventory protection elsewhere.

The current printing area appears to be the bottleneck because queues form there. This means it constrains the throughput of the whole system. Automated printing could therefore improve performance if it genuinely increases the capacity and reliability of this stage. Placing printing and assembly in a product layout for the standard bottles could also reduce the time and labour used moving batches between separate areas. Since demand for this range is high and predictable, a capital-intensive flow process is likely to have sufficient volume to spread its fixed costs. It could produce more good bottles per labour hour, so labour productivity may rise, and fewer hand-offs may reduce waiting and opportunities for errors.

However, production rising would not automatically mean that productivity or efficiency improves. If automation creates defects, requires frequent maintenance or produces stock that cannot be sold, more output would not be more good output. The business must also pay for equipment, specialist maintenance and retraining before it receives the possible benefits. This is particularly important because capital-intensive production is less flexible. The premium personalised range has variable demand and requires variety, so forcing it into the same standardised flow process could reduce its ability to meet customer requirements. A flexible batch process may remain more appropriate for that range.

Lean improvement could strengthen the proposal. Employees may know why printing designs are incorrect and where unnecessary movement occurs. Small, measured improvements could reduce rework, waiting and handling, which would improve efficiency as well as measured labour productivity. Yet lean should not be interpreted as removing every activity that does not directly create a bottle. Maintenance, training and a limited capacity buffer may be necessary to prevent breakdowns and cope with peaks. Operating at maximum utilisation could leave no room to recover from a demand surge or equipment failure, causing longer queues and poorer customer service.

Reducing raw-material inventory could release cash and reduce storage costs. This would support efficiency if inventory is genuinely excessive. Nevertheless, deliveries closer to need make production more dependent on suppliers arriving on time. As a key supplier has already delivered late several times, a strict just-in-time approach could stop the new flow line and cause stock-outs. The apparent saving in inventory may then be outweighed by lost sales, idle equipment and damaged customer relationships. Harbour Homeware should retain a suitable buffer stock or develop a backup supplier before reducing inventory substantially.

Overall, Harbour Homeware should approve a staged implementation. It should first target the printing bottleneck and trial automation and a product layout for the stable, standard range. It should measure good output, rework, downtime, waiting time and service performance, rather than relying only on headline output. A lean programme involving employees is worthwhile, but reduced inventory should be gradual and conditional on better supplier reliability. This approach is more likely to improve productivity and efficiency while preserving the flexibility and resilience needed for the premium range and uncertain supply conditions.

Northstar Home Systems sells smart heating controls through national retailers and directly to household customers. It has grown from one UK site to operations in the UK, France and Germany. The business is organised mainly by function: sales, marketing, production, software, customer service and finance all report to the UK head office.

Product launches have been delayed because country sales managers say that software and production teams do not respond quickly to local customer feedback. Head office approval is required for all price changes, marketing campaigns and customer compensation above £100. This has protected a consistent brand, but local managers say that competitors respond faster.

Northstar will introduce automated testing equipment within 12 months. The equipment will reduce routine testing work but will require more employees who can analyse software faults and maintain automated systems. Some experienced testers could be retrained, while others may not have suitable roles after the change. The chief executive is considering product-based divisions with more decision-making delegated to country managers.
output.stem: Evaluate whether Northstar Home Systems should replace its functional structure with product-based divisions and decentralise more decisions to country managers. In your answer, recommend how Northstar should plan its workforce for the introduction of automated testing, including the appropriate use of recruitment, training, redeployment and, where necessary, redundancy.

levels.descriptor: Shows limited knowledge of organisational structure, decision authority or workforce planning. Application to Northstar is weak or largely asserted. Analysis is undeveloped, with little or no supported judgement.

Shows some relevant knowledge and applies it to Northstar. Explains some likely effects of changing structure, decentralising decisions or managing the testing workforce, although analysis may be one-sided or incomplete. A judgement may be present but is not well justified.

Shows clear knowledge of relevant organisational design and workforce-planning concepts. Develops logical chains of analysis linked to Northstar's international growth, slow response and automation. Considers more than one option or consequence and reaches a reasoned, though not fully sustained, judgement.

Shows good, accurate and well-selected knowledge. Analyses the interdependence between structure, decision rights, coordination and workforce capability in Northstar's circumstances. Evaluates significant trade-offs, including the risks and benefits of retraining, redeployment, recruitment and redundancy. The judgement is well supported and considers conditions or implementation.

Shows thorough and precise knowledge integrated throughout a focused response. Sustains detailed, context-specific analysis of structural and workforce choices, including their limitations and likely implementation challenges. Makes a balanced and convincing judgement that prioritises decisions and actions, recognises relevant uncertainty, and is clearly supported by the evidence in the stimulus.

indicative_content: A functional structure can provide specialist expertise, standardisation and central control. This may help Northstar maintain one brand and coordinate technical standards across countries.

However, Northstar's separate functions may create slower cross-functional coordination. Local feedback may pass through several departments and head office before production or software changes are made, contributing to delayed product launches.

Product-based divisions could create clearer accountability for the performance and development of each product range. Bringing relevant sales, marketing, software and production expertise closer together could improve coordination and speed of innovation.

Product-based divisions may duplicate specialist staff or create rivalry between divisions. This could raise costs and make technical standards less consistent, especially where products share software or production resources.

Decentralising selected decisions to country managers could allow faster local responses to competitor price changes, campaigns and customer complaints. It would make greater use of local knowledge in France and Germany.

Decentralisation could also cause inconsistent pricing, promotions or customer outcomes. Country managers need sufficient capability, information and clear limits; otherwise decisions may conflict with the brand or reduce profitability.

Northstar need not treat centralisation as an all-or-nothing choice. It could centralise product safety, core software standards, investment and brand rules, while delegating bounded local pricing, campaign adaptation and customer compensation decisions.

A change in organisation chart alone will not solve delays. Northstar needs clear decision rights, escalation rules, shared information and coordination between product divisions, countries and central specialists.
Workforce planning should start with the work and capabilities required after automation, rather than automatically replacing employees who leave or assuming that all routine testers will be removed.

Automation changes task requirements: routine testing demand may fall, while fault analysis, software capability and equipment maintenance become more important. Northstar should identify the scale, timing and location of these capability gaps.

Training can enable suitable existing testers to operate, maintain or interpret results from the automated equipment. It preserves organisational knowledge and can support morale and retention, but it will work only if employees have the aptitude, time and opportunities to apply the new skills.

Redeployment may be appropriate where testers can move, following development, to fault analysis, quality improvement, customer-support feedback or other roles. It can retain experience and avoid some redundancy costs, but the available role must be genuine and suitable.

External recruitment may be needed where Northstar lacks specialist automation maintenance or software-fault analysis skills and cannot develop them quickly enough. It can bring new expertise but has search, onboarding and uncertainty costs.

Redundancy may be necessary if routine testing roles genuinely disappear and suitable redeployment is unavailable. It can reduce long-run labour costs, but creates payment and consultation obligations, risks loss of knowledge and may damage morale among remaining employees.

The preferred approach depends on the urgency of automation, the transferability of current testers' skills, availability of specialist labour, the cost and time of development, and Northstar's need to maintain product quality during transition.

A supported judgement could recommend a phased hybrid approach: retain central control over high-risk and brand-critical decisions, delegate specified local commercial decisions, pilot product-based coordination, conduct a skills audit, retrain and redeploy viable testers, recruit scarce expertise, and use redundancy only after fair consideration of alternatives.
mark_scheme.model_answer:
Northstar should not simply replace its functional structure with fully independent product divisions and decentralise every decision. Its current functional structure has benefits because software, production and other specialists can apply common standards across the UK, France and Germany. This is particularly important for a smart heating product where consistent technical and safety standards matter. Central approval may also prevent country managers from making price or compensation decisions that weaken margins or damage a consistent brand.

However, the current arrangement appears increasingly unsuitable for Northstar's growth. Customer feedback from France or Germany must move through country managers, head office and separate functional departments before action is taken. This can delay product launches because no product-focused team has clear responsibility for joining up local market information, software changes and production decisions. Product-based divisions could improve accountability and cross-functional coordination: staff working on a particular product range could respond more quickly to faults and customer needs.

The disadvantage is that product divisions could duplicate software, marketing or production expertise. They may also compete for resources and develop inconsistent solutions. Therefore, Northstar should use a hybrid arrangement rather than fully separate divisions. Product-focused teams should coordinate development and launch decisions, but central specialists should retain responsibility for core software architecture, technical standards, major investment and the overall brand.

Similarly, decentralisation should be selective. Country managers are likely to have better information about local competitors and customer expectations, so delegated limits for local promotions, small price changes and customer compensation could improve response speed. This is likely to be particularly valuable because competitors are currently responding faster. Yet unrestricted local authority could make prices and customer treatment inconsistent. Northstar should set decision limits, provide data and require escalation for larger discounts, major campaigns and decisions that affect product standards. Delegation would then speed routine local decisions without removing central accountability.

Automation means that workforce planning must focus on future capability, not merely cutting the number of testers. Demand for routine testing is likely to fall, but demand for employees able to maintain equipment and analyse software faults will increase. Northstar should first conduct a skills audit to identify which testers can be trained for these roles. Training and redeployment would retain valuable knowledge of product faults and may reduce the morale damage and cost associated with dismissals. However, training is not automatically effective: employees need the aptitude for technical roles, managers must provide opportunities to use the new skills, and the business must address any process problems created by the new equipment.

Where there is an immediate shortage of specialist automation or software expertise, external recruitment may be necessary because waiting for all employees to develop could jeopardise quality and the automation timetable. Nevertheless, recruitment has cost and uncertainty, so it should target genuinely scarce capabilities rather than replace every tester automatically. If some routine roles disappear and no suitable redeployment exists after fair consideration, redundancy may be unavoidable. It would lower long-run labour costs, but Northstar should recognise consultation and payment obligations, possible loss of experience and weaker morale among remaining employees.

Overall, Northstar should adopt product-focused coordination with controlled decentralisation, rather than a complete break from functional central control. This directly addresses slow local response while protecting common standards. Its workforce plan should prioritise skills analysis, training and redeployment, supplemented by targeted external recruitment. Redundancy should be a last resort where automation has removed a role and a suitable alternative cannot be provided. The success of both changes will depend on clear authority boundaries, capable country managers and sufficient time for employees to acquire the required technical skills.

Hearth & Home Ltd is a UK retailer of kitchen equipment with 18 stores and an online operation. Sales have grown through product range extensions, but the business has recently experienced stock shortages and longer delivery times. Customers typically pay when ordering online, while suppliers allow Hearth & Home 30 days to pay.

The board is considering two growth options. Option 1 is organic growth: opening six further stores over two years and expanding the online range. This would allow the business to recruit and train staff gradually, but new stores would take time to build customer awareness.

Option 2 is to acquire CookPro Ltd, a smaller retailer with 12 stores, an established customer base and a separate distribution network. The acquisition would provide immediate additional outlets and could create purchasing economies of scale through larger orders to suppliers. Directors also claim that duplicated head-office roles and distribution facilities could be removed. However, CookPro uses different stock-control systems, has a more centralised management style and requires a substantial purchase price. Some directors are concerned that rapidly combining the two businesses could create coordination problems and place pressure on cash if inventory has to be increased before the businesses' operations are integrated.

A third proposal is to close four poorly performing Hearth & Home stores and use the released resources to improve the online operation before pursuing either growth option.
output.stem: Evaluate whether Hearth & Home Ltd should acquire CookPro Ltd rather than pursue organic growth.

levels.descriptor: Shows limited knowledge of growth methods and/or scale. Application to Hearth & Home is weak or absent. Assertions about the acquisition or organic growth are generic, with little developed reasoning or judgement.

Shows some relevant knowledge of organic and external growth, economies or diseconomies of scale, synergy, cash pressure or retrenchment. There is some application to the business, although reasoning may be one-sided, incomplete or based on undeveloped chains. A judgement may be present but is unsupported or inconsistent.

Shows sound knowledge and application to the circumstances of Hearth & Home. Analyses relevant advantages and risks of acquisition and organic growth, using developed causal chains. Evaluation is evident through consideration of conditions, trade-offs or limitations, leading to a supported, though not fully developed, judgement.

Shows strong, accurate and well-focused knowledge applied throughout. Analysis explains how the acquisition could create scale economies or synergy, while also examining integration, coordination, finance, cash and operational risks. Evaluation is balanced and prioritises factors that are material to the decision. The judgement is clear and well justified.

Shows comprehensive and consistently relevant knowledge, application, analysis and evaluation. Develops convincing, interconnected reasoning across growth method, scale, integration and financial/operational constraints. Makes a nuanced judgement that is explicitly conditional on strategic fit, realistic synergy delivery, management capacity and sustainable working-capital finance, while considering the role of retrenchment or staged organic growth.

indicative_content: Organic growth is internal expansion. It may be slower than acquisition, but Hearth & Home could open stores and develop the online range in stages, allowing gradual recruitment, training and learning.

An acquisition is external growth through obtaining control of another business. Buying CookPro would give Hearth & Home immediate access to 12 stores, customers and a distribution network, potentially increasing market presence more quickly than opening six stores.

The larger combined purchasing volume could create purchasing economies of scale if suppliers offer bulk discounts or improved terms. This could lower long-run average cost, improving competitiveness or margins.

Removing genuinely duplicated head-office roles or distribution facilities could create cost synergy. However, synergy is not automatic: the business must identify which activities overlap, whether closure costs are manageable and whether service can be maintained.

CookPro's separate distribution network may provide capacity and capability, but different stock-control systems could make integration difficult. Poor system integration could worsen stock shortages or delivery times rather than solve them.

A more centralised management style at CookPro could clash with Hearth & Home's existing approach. Additional management layers, communication difficulties and slower decision-making could create diseconomies of scale, increasing long-run average cost or damaging responsiveness.

The acquisition price may reduce financial flexibility. If the combined business needs additional inventory while operations are being integrated, cash can be tied up before all expected benefits are achieved.

Growth can create overtrading risk: increased activity may require more inventory and other operating resources before the benefits of additional sales are realised. Profit or sales growth would not by itself demonstrate that the acquisition is affordable or sustainable.

Organic growth may avoid a large immediate purchase price and enables staged investment, but may leave Hearth & Home with continuing stock shortages if it does not first address operational capacity and stock control.

Closing the four poorly performing stores is retrenchment: a strategic reduction in scope or capacity. It could release resources and management attention for the online operation, but may also reduce sales, local presence and potential scale economies.

The best decision depends on whether CookPro's purchase price is justified by achievable benefits, whether systems and cultures can be integrated, whether working-capital finance is available, and whether management can resolve current service problems.

A reasoned conclusion may support acquisition only after due diligence and a credible integration and cash plan; alternatively, it may favour retrenchment and staged organic online growth if current operational weaknesses and financial risk are the binding constraints.
mark_scheme.model_answer:
Hearth & Home could benefit from acquiring CookPro because it would gain 12 established stores, customers and a distribution network immediately. This is likely to be faster than organic growth, where the six proposed stores would need time to become known to customers. The acquisition could also create purchasing economies of scale. If the combined business places larger orders with suppliers, it may obtain lower input costs or better terms, reducing long-run average cost. In addition, there may be synergy if genuinely duplicated head-office roles or distribution facilities can be removed.

However, these benefits are uncertain. Synergy is not created simply because the two businesses are combined. CookPro has different stock-control systems, and Hearth & Home already has stock shortages and delivery delays. Combining systems poorly could create a bottleneck in operations, leading to further stockouts, dissatisfied customers and weaker repeat purchasing. The different management styles could also make coordination slower and create diseconomies of scale through extra communication and management complexity. Therefore, the claimed cost savings may be offset by integration costs and lower service quality.

The financial risk is particularly important. The acquisition requires a substantial purchase price, reducing financial flexibility. Growth may also require more inventory before the combined operation is running efficiently. Although customers pay when ordering online, supplier credit lasts only 30 days, so inventory and other operating needs could still create cash pressure. If activity expands faster than available working-capital finance, Hearth & Home could overtrade: sales may rise while liquidity becomes increasingly fragile.

Organic growth would be slower, but it would allow the business to recruit, train and invest in capacity progressively. This could be preferable because it gives management time to correct the existing stock and delivery problems before adding further complexity. Closing the four weak stores could also release resources for the online operation. Nevertheless, retrenchment could reduce sales and geographic presence, so it should be used only where the stores are unlikely to become viable.

Overall, Hearth & Home should not acquire CookPro simply to grow quickly. Acquisition is preferable only if due diligence shows that the purchase price is affordable, supplier and distribution savings are specific and achievable, and management has a realistic plan to integrate systems without worsening service. Given its current operational weaknesses and potential cash pressure, a staged approach is likely to be safer: first improve stock control and consider closing persistently weak stores, then pursue organic online growth. The acquisition could become attractive later if it provides clear, financeable synergies and the business has the managerial capacity to integrate it successfully.

output.stem: Using the shared stimulus, analyse why Mend & Move’s owners may find it difficult to decide whether revenue growth, profit per order or maintaining sufficient cash should be their greatest priority in the next year. Your answer should consider the business’s stated purpose.

levels.descriptor: Shows limited understanding of one or more objectives or financial measures. Makes simple statements about the stimulus, with little or no developed link between an objective and its consequences for Mend & Move.
Shows sound understanding of objectives, revenue, profit and/or cash. Applies this to Mend & Move and develops some linked analysis of why prioritising one objective can affect another.

Shows thorough, well-focused understanding of the business’s purpose and potentially conflicting objectives. Develops clear chains of analysis using the stimulus to explain the trade-offs between revenue growth, profit per order and cash, including how the proposed system could affect these priorities.

indicative_content: Mend & Move’s purpose is to make lower-waste cleaning products convenient and affordable for busy households. Its objectives should guide resource allocation and should be consistent with this broad purpose.

Revenue growth could support the purpose if subscriptions, faster dispatch and personalised reminders make refills more convenient and attract more customers. Revenue has already risen from £1.35m to £1.80m as online subscriptions have grown.

Higher revenue does not automatically mean higher profit. Profit is revenue remaining after relevant costs, so increased orders could reduce profit per order if personalised communication, training, delivery, financing or system-related costs rise faster than revenue.

Protecting profit per order could support financial sustainability and help fund future activity. However, reducing expenditure too strongly could weaken delivery speed, app quality or customer convenience, which may conflict with the business’s purpose and make it harder to overcome customers’ view that refills are less convenient than supermarket brands.
Cash should be prioritised because only £85,000 is held at year end and the business needs to pay suppliers on time. Cash has already fallen because of advance sachet purchases and delivery crates.

The proposed system requires £120,000 from cash, exceeding the reported year-end cash balance if considered in isolation. This illustrates the tension between preserving liquidity and investing to improve future speed, accuracy, waste reduction and demand forecasting.

A £120,000 bank loan may preserve some cash compared with fully cash-funded investment, but creates a future financial obligation and could put pressure on profit. The system may also require staff training and changes to warehouse roles.

The owners face a trade-off: prioritising immediate cash may reduce financial risk but delay a system that could increase convenience and future revenue; prioritising growth and investment may improve long-term value creation but heighten short-term cash and implementation risk.

Relevant analysis may recognise that objectives can be complementary as well as conflicting: better demand forecasts could reduce wasted stock and picking errors, potentially supporting cash, profit and customer convenience. These gains are uncertain because inaccurate data, system failures or poor recommendations could damage trust.
mark_scheme.model_answer:
Mend & Move has difficulty selecting one priority because its objectives are connected but can conflict. Its purpose is to make lower-waste cleaning products convenient and affordable, so revenue growth is not simply a financial target. The automated system could make ordering and dispatch more convenient through personalised reminders and faster packing. This may encourage subscription demand and help the business respond to customers who value home delivery, increasing revenue from its current £1.80m level.

However, revenue growth is not the same as profit growth. Profit is what remains after costs, and the system could increase costs through staff training, changed warehouse roles and borrowing. If these costs rise more than the additional revenue or if recommendations are ineffective, profit per order could fall. Conversely, demand forecasting and fewer picking errors could reduce wasted stock and operating inefficiencies, which could protect profit per order. Therefore, the profit objective depends on whether the expected operational improvements are achieved.

Maintaining cash is also important because the business holds only £85,000 and needs enough liquidity to pay suppliers on time. The proposed funding includes £120,000 from cash, while cash has already fallen after buying stock in advance and delivery crates. Giving cash the greatest priority would reduce the risk of payment difficulties, but delaying the system could leave refills less convenient than supermarket alternatives and restrict future revenue growth. The owners must therefore balance short-term cash security against investment that could support convenience, lower waste and future profitability, rather than assuming that the highest revenue target should automatically dominate.

output.stem: Using the case study, evaluate whether Mend & Move Refill Co. should proceed with the proposed automated packing and demand-forecasting system. In your answer, consider how technological change and changing customer lifestyles may affect the decision, alongside the interests of relevant stakeholders.

levels.descriptor: Shows limited knowledge of technology, online buying behaviour or stakeholder interests. Application to Mend & Move is weak or mainly copied from the case study. Analysis is asserted rather than developed, and any judgement is unsupported.

Shows some relevant understanding and application to the proposed system. Explains one or more possible benefits or drawbacks, such as faster dispatch, improved forecasting, training needs or customer trust. A conclusion is present but is generic, one-sided or weakly justified.

Shows clear, relevant understanding of technological change, customer lifestyle change and stakeholder effects. Analyses linked consequences for Mend & Move, including how the system could affect convenience, operations, costs, cash or trust. Makes a supported judgement that recognises a relevant limitation, risk or trade-off.

Shows thorough and well-focused understanding throughout. Develops balanced chains of analysis using the specific circumstances of Mend & Move, including the fit between the technology, online subscription customers and operational objectives. Evaluates material uncertainties, implementation capability, stakeholder conflicts and the financial/cash constraint. Reaches a well-supported, contextual judgement, with clear conditions or an alternative course of action where appropriate.

indicative_content: The system is a process and digital-service innovation rather than merely a software purchase. Value depends on successful implementation, staff training, reliable customer-order data and changed warehouse processes.

Mend & Move's target households value home delivery and managing subscriptions by mobile phone. Personalised reminders and faster dispatch could make refills more convenient, addressing the concern that refills are less convenient than supermarket brands.

Better demand forecasts could reduce over-ordering of refill sachets, reduce wasted stock and improve availability. Fewer picking errors may improve customer experience, retention and repeat subscription revenue.

Reduced packaging waste may support Mend & Move's lower-waste purpose. However, the business should avoid assuming that an environmental benefit is proven without evidence across its operations and supply chain.

The business operates in a growing online refill-subscription market. The system may help it respond to the wider move towards online shopping, but market growth alone does not prove that customers will value or respond positively to personalised app communication.

Inaccurate data or unsuitable recommendations could inconvenience customers and reduce trust. System failures could delay dispatch, creating a particularly serious risk because convenience is central to the proposition and customers can compare alternatives online.

Warehouse staff may require training and some roles may change. Better productivity could support profit per order, but disruption, resistance or inadequate skills could delay benefits and harm employee relations.

Owners seek revenue growth, profit per order and sufficient cash, but these objectives conflict. The £240,000 investment is partly funded from cash when year-end cash is only £85,000 and has already fallen because of advance stock purchases and delivery crates.

The £120,000 bank loan creates repayment and financing obligations. This may put pressure on cash even if the system eventually improves efficiency; the six-month implementation period means benefits are uncertain and may not be immediate.

A staged implementation, pilot of personalised reminders, staff consultation and testing of data quality could reduce the risk of a full rollout. These actions may preserve flexibility but could slow the benefits.

A justified conclusion may support proceeding only if Mend & Move protects supplier-payment capacity and tests the system before full implementation. Alternatively, delaying the investment could be justified if the immediate cash risk is judged more severe than the likely operational gains.
mark_scheme.model_answer:
Mend & Move has a strong strategic reason to proceed because the proposed system could make its subscription offer more convenient for its main customers. Its target group values home delivery and uses mobile phones to manage subscriptions, while interviews suggest that some potential customers currently regard refills as less convenient than supermarket products. Faster dispatch and personalised refill reminders could therefore reduce missed or late orders. This could increase repeat purchases and revenue, rather than simply relying on growth in the refill-subscription market.

The system could also improve operational performance. Forecasting demand from customer-order data may allow Mend & Move to buy refill sachets more accurately, reducing excess stock and packaging waste. Fewer picking errors could reduce replacement and customer-service costs, helping to protect profit per order. This would support both the business's lower-waste purpose and its financial objectives. However, these outcomes are not automatic. The business will gain little from the technology if staff are not trained, warehouse processes are not redesigned, or the customer data produces inaccurate forecasts. In that case, stock availability and dispatch could worsen rather than improve.

There are significant stakeholder and financial risks. Customers may welcome reminders, but poor recommendations or system failures could damage trust, especially because convenience is a key reason for choosing the service. Employees may benefit from training and fewer errors, but changing warehouse roles could create resistance or disruption. Most importantly, cash is only £85,000 at the year end, yet £120,000 of the investment would come from cash. Although the other £120,000 is borrowed, loan repayments could further constrain cash. Mend & Move must still pay suppliers on time after already tying up cash in advance purchases of sachets.

Overall, Mend & Move should proceed, but not as an immediate uncontrolled full rollout. The technology fits changing online lifestyles and could address the convenience weakness in its offer, so delaying indefinitely risks losing customers as the market grows. However, the owners should first test the forecasting and reminder functions, train affected staff and ensure that the funding plan leaves enough cash to meet supplier payments. This conditional approach is preferable because it captures the potential long-term revenue and efficiency gains while limiting the most serious short-term risk: damaging customer trust or creating a cash shortfall during the six-month implementation period.
