Herzberg argued that motivators, rather than hygiene factors, create job satisfaction. Giving assembly employees responsibility for quality checks and for suggesting process improvements increases responsibility and recognition, which are motivators. Employees may feel that their judgement matters and gain greater achievement from completing a unit to the required standard. This could make the repetitive task more meaningful, increase job satisfaction and reduce staff turnover. In turn, more motivated employees may take greater care over assembly quality and remain with Kestrel Kitchens for longer.

A representative consultation group would give employees a formal way to communicate their concerns about childcare and travel directly to managers before the shift changes are finalised. Representatives can gather views from different employees, so managers are more likely to understand practical problems caused by weekend working.

This two-way communication may improve trust because employees can see that management is listening rather than imposing a decision. Managers may then amend shift patterns, for example by considering employees’ circumstances, which could make the final decision seem fairer. Employees are therefore more likely to accept the changes and cooperate with them, reducing conflict and improving employee relations.

Final inspection identifies faulty containers after production, shortly before dispatch. It can prevent some loose lids or cracked seals from being sent to customers, but it does not stop the defects being made in the first place. Defective containers may already have used materials and labour and may need to be reworked or discarded.

Quality assurance is different because it aims to prevent defects during the production process. Training staff, using standardised machine settings and carrying out checks while containers are being made should reduce the likelihood of loose lids and cracked seals occurring. This should lead to more consistent output and fewer defective containers reaching customers.

As a result, Harbour Homeware may experience fewer returns and online complaints. Customer satisfaction and the business’s reputation could improve, potentially helping it retain customers. The firm could also reduce the cost of waste, rework and handling returned containers, improving efficiency.

However, quality assurance requires staff training and production checks, which may increase costs initially and could slow production while employees adapt to the new procedures. Its success will depend on staff consistently following the settings and checks. Nevertheless, unlike relying only on final inspection, effective quality assurance tackles the causes of defects rather than only detecting them at the end.

Becoming a plc would allow Northton Foods to issue shares to the public and potentially raise substantial finance for the new production site. This may be more suitable than relying on a large long-term loan because share capital does not have to be repaid in the same way as borrowing. The business could use the funds to build the site without creating large loan repayments, which may reduce pressure on cash flow while the new site is being developed.

A successful share issue could also enable the business to raise more finance than the two founders could provide themselves. If the new site increases production capacity successfully, Northton Foods may be better able to meet demand and grow.

However, issuing shares would dilute the founders’ ownership. As public shareholders buy shares, the founders may no longer have the same level of control over decisions. Shareholders may also expect dividends and may judge the directors on the company’s performance, increasing pressure on the founders.

Becoming a plc can therefore provide the substantial, long-term finance needed without a large loan, but it involves giving up some control and taking on obligations to public shareholders. Whether it is preferable depends on whether the founders value retaining control more highly than accessing the finance for the new site.

Northshore should adopt a predominantly soft HRM approach, although it should retain some hard HRM controls. Soft HRM treats employees as an important resource to develop and involve, whereas hard HRM focuses more on staffing targets, standardisation, close measurement and labour-cost control.

A soft approach is likely to help Northshore address the loss of experienced technicians. Offering development, career opportunities and flexible working could make the business more attractive to applicants with different expectations. It may also improve retention, as existing employees may feel that the business is investing in them rather than treating them only as a cost. This matters because the business needs software technicians, installers and customer-support staff within 18 months. Retaining skilled employees reduces the risk that Northshore recruits people but then continues to lose experienced staff before the new range is launched.

Training and employee involvement are especially relevant because the product range uses new technology. Consulting employees on job design may identify what skills are required in each role and could improve the design of training. Technicians, installers and support employees may have useful knowledge about the practical problems customers experience. Involving employee representatives in major changes could also improve acceptance of new working practices. This should support the objective of employees acting consistently with customer-care values, since employees are more likely to understand and support values that have been communicated and discussed.

Soft HRM could also help workforce diversity. Flexible working and consultation may widen the range of people willing and able to apply. A more diverse workforce could give Northshore access to a broader talent pool when it needs employees in two locations. This is particularly valuable where applicants have varied backgrounds and expectations. If the business instead applies rigid procedures and focuses mainly on low labour costs, it may discourage potentially suitable candidates or fail to retain them.

However, a predominantly hard HRM approach has some advantages. Northshore has a clear deadline of 18 months and needs sufficient numbers of several employee groups across two locations. Precise staffing plans would help ensure that it does not have too few installers, technicians or support employees when the product is launched. Measuring output can identify delays and allow managers to respond quickly. Fixed procedures may also promote consistent customer service, particularly where employees deal with installation or customer queries. Keeping labour costs under control is important because extensive training, flexible arrangements and development opportunities could be expensive.

The main limitation of relying mainly on hard HRM is that it may diagnose the service-delay problem incorrectly. Managers already believe that unclear workflows and unsuitable software, rather than employee effort alone, may cause some delays. Tighter individual targets could place pressure on employees without solving these operational problems. This could reduce engagement and make experienced staff more likely to leave. Therefore, hard HRM may deliver apparent short-term control while damaging the talent pipeline and customer-care culture required for the new range.

There are also limits to soft HRM. Consultation can take time, and different employee preferences may make it difficult to design jobs and flexible-working arrangements that meet operational requirements. Northshore cannot allow flexibility to leave customer-support shifts uncovered or installer capacity insufficient. Development opportunities will not automatically improve performance if workflows remain unclear or software is unsuitable. Soft HRM must therefore be accompanied by investment in appropriate systems and clear responsibilities.

Overall, Northshore should use a predominantly soft HRM approach because its most significant challenges are retaining expertise, recruiting from a broad pool, developing new technical skills and creating engagement with customer-care values. These objectives depend heavily on employee commitment rather than simply on controlling labour costs. Nevertheless, the approach should be supported by hard HRM elements: workforce planning for each location, clear service standards, and proportionate performance measures. Management should first clarify workflows and improve unsuitable software, then use employee consultation and training to build capability. This balanced approach is more likely to achieve both reliable service and a sustainable workforce for the launch.

Harbour Homeware should implement much of the proposal, but it should introduce it gradually and protect itself against supplier and capacity risks.

A product layout with automated printing and assembly is likely to improve efficiency for the standard range. Demand for this range is high and relatively predictable, so a flow process can be used consistently. At present, products move between cutting, printing and assembly areas, creating time spent handling stock rather than adding value. Putting equipment in a product layout should reduce movement, waiting time and work-in-progress. Automation may also reduce printing errors, so fewer batches need rework. This would raise productivity because more saleable bottles could be produced from the same employee time and materials.

The existing printing area is a bottleneck because it creates queues. Improving printing capacity through automation could increase the throughput of the whole standard-range process. However, the business should not assume that installing faster printing alone will solve the problem. If assembly cannot match the new printing output, the bottleneck may simply move to assembly. The proposed combined automated printing and assembly equipment is therefore more suitable than improving just one department, as it may create a smoother flow. Managers should test whether cutting, material supply and final dispatch can also support the increased rate of output.

The major disadvantage is the substantial initial investment. Automated equipment, specialist maintenance and retraining increase fixed costs. The investment is more likely to be worthwhile when output is high and stable, which fits the standard range. If demand for standard bottles fell, high fixed costs would still have to be paid and the equipment could be underused. It would be less appropriate to use this rigid product layout for the premium personalised range, where demand changes frequently and flexibility is important. Harbour Homeware should retain a more flexible batch process for premium products rather than attempting to force both ranges through one system.

A lean programme could further raise efficiency. Smaller batch sizes would reduce the amount of stock waiting between stages and could reveal problems, such as incorrect printed designs, more quickly. Employee suggestions may be valuable because employees directly observe causes of delays, waste and quality problems. Reducing storage space and releasing cash tied up in inventory would also improve the use of working capital. These benefits are particularly significant because current queues and unnecessary stock movement indicate waste in the existing process.

However, lower raw-material inventory creates a serious risk. One key supplier has already made several late deliveries. Delivering materials close to when they are needed could cause a stock-out and stop a capital-intensive flow line. The lost output, late customer orders and idle employees could outweigh the savings from holding less inventory. Lean operations depend on reliable suppliers and accurate coordination, neither of which is guaranteed by the information provided. Harbour Homeware should therefore improve supplier reliability, perhaps by agreeing clearer delivery expectations or reducing reliance on a single key supplier, before moving fully to just-in-time deliveries.

Capacity also needs careful management. Removing all spare capacity would make the business vulnerable during demand peaks, equipment downtime or supplier delays. Since the new equipment requires specialist maintenance, unexpected breakdowns could stop the whole flow process. Some spare capacity and a planned maintenance programme are justified, even though they may appear inefficient in the short term. Holding a limited buffer of critical raw materials would also be sensible while supplier late deliveries continue.

Overall, Harbour Homeware should invest in automated flow production for the predictable, high-demand standard range because it directly addresses stock movement, the printing bottleneck and rework. It should not apply the same process to the variable premium personalised range. The lean programme should be phased in, with smaller batches and employee improvement ideas introduced first, but inventory levels should only be reduced to the point that service reliability is maintained. The final decision depends on whether expected productivity and quality gains from the standard-range equipment are sufficient to cover the investment, maintenance and retraining costs, while maintaining enough capacity and inventory resilience to avoid costly stoppages.

Northstar has clear reasons to change its structure. Its functional structure gives UK head office control over sales, marketing, production, software, customer service and finance. This can protect brand consistency and allow specialist expertise, for example software engineers can be managed together and testing standards can be consistent across countries. Central approval of prices, campaigns and compensation also reduces the risk of local managers making costly or inconsistent decisions.

However, the evidence suggests that the existing structure is becoming too slow. Sales managers in France and Germany receive local customer feedback, but software and production teams are controlled through head office. Delayed product launches could therefore cause Northstar to lose sales to competitors that react faster. Product-based divisions could bring employees from marketing, software, production and customer service closer to the relevant product decisions. This should improve communication, make responsibility for a product clearer and speed up changes following customer feedback.

Decentralising selected decisions to country managers would also be beneficial. They understand local customer needs and competitive conditions better than a UK head office. For example, allowing managers to make smaller price adjustments, approve local campaigns within an agreed budget and settle more customer complaints could improve responsiveness and customer service. Faster resolution of compensation claims may protect Northstar's reputation with direct household customers as well as retailers.

Nevertheless, fully replacing the functional structure with product-based divisions could create problems. If each division has its own software, production and testing staff, Northstar may duplicate expensive specialist employees across the UK, France and Germany. This would be particularly risky during automation, when employees able to analyse software faults and maintain automated systems are likely to be scarce. Separate divisions might also develop inconsistent quality standards, prices and marketing messages, weakening the consistent brand that centralisation has protected. Product divisions would be most appropriate if Northstar has sufficiently different products with different customer needs; the case only identifies smart heating controls, so the benefits of full divisionalisation are uncertain.

Northstar should therefore adopt a more gradual hybrid approach rather than immediately abolishing all functions. It could retain central functional centres of expertise for production, software, finance and automated-testing standards, while creating product-focused cross-functional teams. These teams should include country sales and marketing input and have clear responsibility for responding to customer feedback and launch deadlines. Country managers should receive delegated authority within defined limits, such as approved price ranges, campaign budgets and a higher but controlled compensation threshold. Head office should continue to approve decisions that could materially affect brand positioning, product safety, major investment or overall profitability. This would gain much of the speed of decentralisation while limiting inconsistency and duplicated expertise.

Workforce planning for automated testing should begin immediately because the equipment will be introduced within 12 months. Northstar should first complete a skills audit of current testers and related software and production employees. It should identify which employees can be trained to maintain automated equipment, interpret test data and diagnose software faults, and compare this with the number of employees needed after automation. It should also consult employees and managers early so that employees understand that routine testing work will fall but higher-skilled technical work will increase.

Training should be the main initial response for experienced testers who have the aptitude to move into fault analysis, automated-system maintenance or quality-assurance roles. Their existing knowledge of Northstar's products and testing processes makes retraining likely to be faster and less risky than replacing all of them. Training could include technical instruction on the new equipment, software diagnostic skills and problem-solving. Employees should be assessed after training to ensure they can perform the new roles safely and effectively.

Recruitment should be used selectively where the skills audit identifies gaps that cannot be met in time through training. Northstar may need to recruit experienced automation-maintenance or software-fault-analysis specialists, especially to support installation of the equipment and to coach retrained staff. Recruiting only for these scarce skills avoids unnecessary recruitment costs and prevents Northstar from losing the knowledge held by current experienced testers.

Redeployment should be considered for employees whose routine testing roles disappear but who do not suit the new technical posts. Possible opportunities may exist in customer service, production support, quality administration or the new product-focused teams, provided employees have transferable skills and receive appropriate training. This helps retain committed employees and reduces redundancy costs, although Northstar should not redeploy people into unsuitable roles simply to avoid difficult decisions.

If, after training, recruitment and genuine redeployment opportunities, there are still more employees than required, redundancy may be necessary. Northstar should use fair, objective selection criteria, consult affected employees and provide notice and support. This is likely to reduce legal, reputational and morale risks. Redundancy should be the final option because it may damage motivation among remaining employees and remove useful product knowledge.

Overall, Northstar should decentralise more operational decisions and use cross-functional product-focused teams, but retain central functional expertise and brand controls. This directly addresses slow responses to local feedback while protecting quality and avoiding costly duplication. Its workforce plan should prioritise skills auditing, retraining and redeployment, supported by targeted recruitment; redundancy should be used only where automation creates a genuine surplus after these alternatives have been considered.

Hearth & Home should be cautious about acquiring CookPro and, on the information available, should favour organic growth, potentially after closing its four poorly performing stores and strengthening its online operation.

An acquisition would deliver growth much faster than organic development. Buying CookPro would immediately increase Hearth & Home's store network from 18 to 30 outlets and bring an established customer base. This is particularly valuable because organically opened stores take time to develop customer awareness. CookPro's separate distribution network could also increase capacity and help address Hearth & Home's current stock shortages and long delivery times. In addition, placing larger combined orders with suppliers may create purchasing economies of scale, reducing unit costs and potentially improving competitiveness or profit margins.

The acquisition could also generate cost savings by removing duplicated head-office posts and distribution facilities. If these savings are achieved quickly, CookPro may provide both revenue growth and lower average costs. Organic growth, by contrast, adds six stores but does not automatically remove existing overheads. Therefore, if CookPro can be bought at a manageable price and its operations can be integrated successfully, acquisition could give Hearth & Home a stronger position much sooner than opening stores gradually.

However, the claimed acquisition benefits are uncertain because the firms have different stock-control systems and management styles. Hearth & Home already has stock shortages, so combining two incompatible stock-control systems could initially make availability and delivery problems worse rather than better. A more centralised CookPro culture may also conflict with Hearth & Home's approach. Staff uncertainty, resistance to changed roles and the removal of duplicated jobs could reduce morale and cause coordination problems. Consequently, the expected economies of scale and head-office savings may take longer to achieve than directors anticipate.

Cash flow is the major risk of acquisition. Although online customers pay when ordering and suppliers give Hearth & Home 30 days' credit, the substantial purchase price must be funded. Further, inventory may need to be increased before operations are integrated, creating an additional cash outflow. Customer receipts and supplier credit help day-to-day working capital, but they may not be sufficient to finance both the purchase and higher inventory. If cash becomes constrained, Hearth & Home may be less able to solve its existing delivery problems or invest in its online operation.

Organic growth is slower, but it is more controllable. Opening six stores over two years allows staff to be recruited and trained gradually, reducing the operational disruption associated with a rapid merger. Management can also adapt stock-control and distribution processes as the online range expands. This is important because improving availability and delivery performance may protect the existing customer base before the business adds more outlets. The disadvantage is that the business would have only 24 stores after two years, whereas acquisition supplies 30 immediately, and new organic stores may initially have weak sales while awareness builds.

The proposal to close four poorly performing stores strengthens the case for a phased organic strategy. Releasing resources from weak outlets could improve the online operation, where customers pay at order and therefore support cash inflows. It would also enable management to resolve the current stock and delivery weaknesses before taking on six new stores. Closing stores could reduce Hearth & Home to 14 stores initially, so it should only close outlets where the released resources and avoided losses exceed the contribution lost. Nevertheless, this approach has lower integration risk than buying another business while existing operations are under pressure.

Overall, Hearth & Home should not acquire CookPro immediately. The immediate scale, customer base and possible purchasing economies are attractive, but they depend on successful integration at a time when Hearth & Home is already experiencing operational problems and faces cash pressure from the purchase price and extra inventory. A more suitable course is to close genuinely poorly performing stores, improve online fulfilment and stock control, then pursue gradual organic expansion. Acquisition could be reconsidered only if detailed due diligence shows that the purchase price is affordable, sufficient cash remains after funding inventory, and the stock systems and management structures can be integrated without worsening customer service.

Mend & Move made a £150,000 profit in 2026, but held only £85,000 cash at the year end. This can occur because it used cash to buy refill sachets in advance and delivery crates. Therefore, a profitable business may still face difficulty paying suppliers on time if too much cash is tied up in stock or assets.

Change in market share = 7.5% − 7.5% = 0 percentage points. Mend & Move grew its sales value, but only at the same rate as the overall market.

The owners face a trade-off because the objectives are connected but can require conflicting decisions. Revenue growth is attractive because the refill-subscription market is expanding and Mend & Move's revenue rose from £1.35m to £1.80m. Growth could spread fixed costs, increase the number of households using subscriptions and help the business achieve its purpose of making lower-waste cleaning convenient and affordable. For example, spending more on app promotion, delivery capacity or introductory offers may persuade busy 25–44-year-old households that refills are as convenient as supermarket brands.

However, prioritising revenue could reduce profit per order. Discounts, free delivery or expensive digital marketing may increase subscription numbers but lower the contribution made by each order. This matters because the owners want to protect profit per order, and the business needs profit to reinvest in service quality and lower-waste packaging. Its profit did rise from £105,000 to £150,000, suggesting growth has so far been profitable, but this does not prove that further rapid growth will remain profitable. Customers attracted mainly by low prices may not accept later price increases, which could make the affordable part of the stated purpose difficult to sustain.

Maintaining cash may be the most immediate constraint. Cash fell from £140,000 to £85,000 despite the business making a profit. Advance purchases of refill sachets and delivery crates used cash before the related sales were received. If Mend & Move focuses on faster growth, it may need still more stock, delivery expenditure and marketing before subscriptions generate cash inflows. It could then struggle to pay suppliers on time, risking interrupted supply and slower deliveries. That would damage convenience for customers and undermine the purpose of making refills convenient.

Conversely, placing cash protection above all else could mean ordering less stock, delaying investment and reducing customer acquisition spending. This may protect short-term liquidity but limit revenue growth while the market is expanding. It could also leave customers with less reliable availability, so they return to established supermarket brands.

The difficulty is therefore timing as well as choice. Revenue growth supports the environmental purpose by replacing single-use plastic, profit per order makes this purpose financially sustainable, and cash is needed to keep operating. The owners should not pursue revenue at any cost: they need growth that produces an adequate profit per order and is paced so that supplier payments can be met.

Mend & Move should proceed only if it can protect liquidity, test the technology before full implementation and show that the expected operational benefits are likely to outweigh the risks. The proposed system fits important changes in both technology and customer lifestyles. More customers are shopping online and the main target group values home delivery and managing subscriptions by mobile phone. Demand forecasting, personalised reminders and faster dispatch could therefore make refills easier to use for busy households. This directly addresses the concern that potential customers see refills as less convenient than buying established brands in supermarkets.

The system could improve competitiveness and support the business's purpose. Better forecasts may reduce excess sachet purchases and packaging waste, while automated packing could reduce picking errors. Fewer incorrect orders and more reliable delivery should raise customer satisfaction and retention. Personalised reminders may reduce the chance that a household runs out of cleaning products, making the refill model more convenient. If these changes increase repeat subscriptions without substantial discounts, Mend & Move may gain revenue while protecting profit per order. Reduced errors and waste could also lower operating costs per order, helping it remain affordable while reducing waste.

The investment could also benefit several stakeholders. Customers may receive more accurate, faster deliveries and useful reminders. Owners may obtain revenue growth, lower waste and stronger differentiation in a growing market. Suppliers could receive more predictable orders if the forecasting system is reliable. The environmental benefit of less packaging waste is consistent with the interests of customers who seek less single-use plastic and with the stated purpose of the business.

However, the financial risk is substantial. The £240,000 investment is large relative to annual revenue of £1.80m, and the planned £120,000 cash contribution exceeds the £85,000 year-end cash balance. Cash has already fallen because of advance sachet purchases and delivery crates. Even though the loan supplies the other £120,000, borrowing will create repayments and interest, increasing pressure on cash and profit per order. A six-month implementation also means that benefits may be delayed while costs are incurred. If forecast demand is wrong, Mend & Move could still hold too much stock, while an automated system failure could delay dispatch and make refill subscriptions appear less convenient than supermarket alternatives.

Stakeholder effects may create further difficulties. Warehouse staff need training and some roles may change. If employees fear job losses or are not trained effectively, resistance, errors during transition or staff turnover could weaken service quality. Poor recommendations or misuse of inaccurate customer data could annoy customers and damage trust in the app. This is especially serious for a subscription business: customers can cancel and buy established brands instead. Owners may also disagree because revenue growth and environmental benefits are uncertain, whereas the cash outflow and debt obligations are more immediate.

A full immediate commitment is not the strongest option. Mend & Move should first run a limited pilot using a smaller customer group or warehouse area, test the accuracy of recommendations and measure changes in picking errors, dispatch time, repeat orders, stock waste and profit per order. It should train and consult affected staff, and retain a contingency process for manual packing if the system fails. It should also prepare cash-flow forecasts that include the £120,000 cash contribution, loan repayments, supplier payments and the possibility that benefits arrive later than expected.

Overall, the system is strategically attractive because changing lifestyles make convenient digital subscriptions increasingly important and the technology could make the lower-waste offer more reliable. Nevertheless, maintaining enough cash to pay suppliers is a stated objective and the proposed cash funding is greater than the reported cash balance. Mend & Move should proceed only in stages, with finance arranged so that working capital is not exhausted and with clear evidence from a pilot that customers respond positively. If it cannot fund the project while maintaining supplier-payment capacity, it should delay or reduce the scope of the investment rather than risk damaging the convenience and trust on which the subscription model depends.

A joint venture would give ParcelPedal local repair capability in the Netherlands. This supports its existing differentiation strategy because Dutch fleet customers buying a reliability-focused product may value rapid local repairs and parts access more than a supplier that simply exports trikes. It could reduce vehicle downtime, making the offer more attractive to delivery fleets and helping the distributor win sales.

The joint venture could also avoid up to £110,000 of export transport and administration costs on the proposed 500 trikes: £220 × 500. Avoiding this cost could protect ParcelPedal's margin, allow a more competitive Dutch price, or fund local service. On this narrow comparison, the £450,000 equity investment is equivalent to about 4.1 years of avoided export costs, before considering any local repair revenues or other joint-venture costs.

In addition, the Dutch partner's influence over product adaptations and local marketing could improve market fit. It may have knowledge of city restrictions, fleet purchasing practices and the requested narrow cargo modules. This should reduce the risk of attempting to sell an unchanged UK-designed product that does not meet local operating needs.

However, these benefits depend on the partner being capable and cooperative. ParcelPedal would share control over adaptations and marketing, so decisions could be slower or could weaken its repairability-based positioning. The saving is also not enough by itself to make the investment attractive quickly. Nevertheless, compared with exporting the current trike, a joint venture offers a stronger local service proposition and potentially lower unit costs, which are especially valuable in a fleet market where downtime matters.

ParcelPedal should proceed with FlexLoad, but only with staged finance and supply-risk controls, because it offers the strongest long-term fit with its differentiation strategy and Dutch growth opportunity.

FlexLoad directly addresses the Dutch requests for removable batteries and narrower modules. It also allows UK fleets to select modules for parcels, groceries or medical supplies. This increases the value of the product for its focused fleet segment, rather than forcing ParcelPedal to compete against RideFast's lower-priced standardised trikes. FlexLoad's forecast contribution is £2,470 per unit after the automated-cell saving. At forecast sales of 1,400 trikes, total contribution would be £3.458m before fixed costs, interest and other innovation-related costs. The £240 unit saving would generate £336,000 of annual cost savings at this volume compared with the pre-automation variable-cost forecast. Lower first-year warranty repairs, from 7% to 3%, should further reinforce the low-downtime positioning and may reduce service costs, although the financial value is not provided.

FlexLoad also makes growth more feasible operationally. Current capacity is 1,400 trikes, while retaining 2024 UK sales and supplying the Dutch order using the existing model would require 1,700 trikes. This is a 300-trike capacity shortfall. FlexLoad raises capacity to 1,600, leaving 200 units of headroom against its 1,400-unit forecast. Therefore, simply prioritising international expansion with the existing design risks either turning away UK customers or failing to supply the Dutch order. Exporting the current model also adds £220 per trike and does not meet the stated Dutch preferences as well as FlexLoad.

Retaining the current model has advantages. It avoids the £2.15m development, tooling and training cost and preserves a proven repairable product and support service. It also avoids dependence on the specialist removable-battery supplier and avoids borrowing. This is significant because ParcelPedal has only £1.10m available cash and needs £1.05m of bank finance. If customers reject the higher £5,650 price, the forecast volume and contribution may not be achieved. The four prototype trials provide some evidence of demand, but they do not guarantee broad acceptance. The patent is also pending, so the modular mounting system may not remain protected from imitation.

A Dutch joint venture using the current design would offer local repairs and could avoid export costs, but it still leaves a weaker product-market fit unless adaptations are made. It also requires £450,000 equity investment and gives the partner influence over product and marketing decisions. Consequently, international expansion alone is a less complete strategy than FlexLoad, although a joint venture could later strengthen FlexLoad's Dutch after-sales service.

Overall, FlexLoad is the best main strategy because it combines product innovation, process efficiency, greater capacity and closer fit with both UK and Dutch fleet needs. The board should approve it only after securing bank finance on acceptable terms, obtaining a robust supply agreement or second-source plan for batteries, and using the Dutch distributor and prototype customers to test willingness to pay before full-scale rollout. If these conditions cannot be met, retaining the current model temporarily would be safer than committing to an unsupported launch.

LoopFill’s 2025 labour turnover was 20.0% (11 leavers ÷ 55 average employees × 100). This is substantially worse than 2024, when turnover was 10.0%, and above the 2025 budgeted 11.1%. High turnover is likely to create recruitment, induction and training costs, while inexperienced replacements may take longer to operate the new automated line effectively. This matters because the additional 50,000-pouch order depends on reliable delivery.

Labour productivity in 2025 was 5,291 good pouches per employee (291,000 ÷ 55). This exceeded both 2024 productivity of 5,100 pouches and the budgeted 5,370 pouches only partially: output was above budget, but employment was also above budget. Therefore, LoopFill has increased output, but has not achieved the labour efficiency planned. A 4.1% absence rate, against a 2.5% budget, could make evening-shift cover difficult and increase bottlenecks, limiting the business’s ability to add the extra order without overtime or temporary staff.

Employee costs were 43.0% of sales revenue (£1,485,000 ÷ £3,450,000 × 100), compared with a budgeted 38.3%. Labour cost per good pouch was £5.10 (£1,485,000 ÷ 291,000), above the budgeted £4.76. Consequently, labour costs have risen faster than output and sales, contributing to operating profit being only £315,000 rather than the £670,000 budget. If turnover and absence persist, covering evening shifts may further raise labour cost per pouch and reduce the profitability of the additional order.

The exit interviews suggest that the issue is not simply evening-shift work: 7 of 11 leavers mentioned shift predictability, but 5 mentioned pay and 4 mentioned training. Better predictable scheduling, relevant training before installation and an appropriate review of pay could reduce departures and absence. This would help retain trained staff, support quality control and make it more likely that the automated line can produce the extra pouches without leaks or customer complaints. However, higher pay and training expenditure could initially worsen LoopFill’s already high employee-cost ratio, so management needs targeted action rather than assuming automation alone will solve the workforce problem.

Accepting the additional order would require LoopFill to supply 50,000 more pouches than its 2025 output of 291,000. This is a 17.2% increase in output, taking total required output to 341,000 pouches. The automated line may reduce evening-shift bottlenecks and enable this capacity increase, but it costs £200,000 before installation and staff must be trained. Delays in installation or training could mean LoopFill cannot meet agreed delivery dates and may lose the additional customer business.

LoopFill cannot safely fund the line from existing cash. It has £95,000 cash but wants to retain an £80,000 buffer because customers normally pay 45 days after delivery. Only £15,000 is available without reducing that buffer, leaving a funding gap of £185,000. This is particularly important because customer receivables have risen to £650,000 while closing cash has fallen to £95,000. Thus, sales may be tied up in unpaid invoices rather than available to pay for the line or day-to-day costs.

The line could improve financial performance if it lowers bottlenecks, reduces labour needed to cover evening shifts and allows profitable sales from the additional order. However, LoopFill’s 2025 financial performance gives reason for caution. Sales revenue was £150,000 below budget and operating profit was £355,000 below budget, despite good-pouch output being 1,000 above budget. This suggests that producing more pouches does not automatically generate the expected revenue or profit. The business must establish the selling price, materials cost, extra labour and any maintenance costs of the additional order before knowing whether the line will generate a satisfactory return.

There is also a quality risk. If faster filling raises pouch leaks or complaints, LoopFill could incur waste, replacement and customer-service costs, and its relationship with its largest customer could be harmed. In contrast, if training and quality controls are effective, the line could allow a higher output without equivalent increases in labour cost and improve the viability of the order. Financially, the investment is therefore potentially necessary for growth, but its return depends on delivery reliability, quality and sufficient contribution from the 50,000 extra pouches.

A bank loan would provide up to the full £200,000 required before installation, allowing LoopFill to retain its £95,000 cash balance and therefore its £80,000 cash buffer. This protects short-term liquidity while customers take around 45 days to pay. The annual interest charge on a £200,000 loan would initially be £14,000, with £40,000 principal repaid each year. Therefore, the initial annual cash commitment would be £54,000. The loan is likely to be manageable if the line and additional order improve cash generation, since current operating profit is £315,000. However, operating profit was far below budget and cash has fallen, so this comparison does not guarantee that cash will be available for repayments. Security over the new line also increases risk: failure to make repayments could threaten the asset needed to meet the order.

Equity crowdfunding avoids contractual interest and principal repayments, which is attractive given high receivables and uncertainty over the additional order’s profitability. It would also spread some risk between the existing owners and new shareholders. However, the 6% platform fee means a £200,000 campaign provides only £188,000 net. LoopFill would need to use £12,000 cash, leaving £83,000, which is only £3,000 above its desired buffer. Crowdfunding would also give investors 18% of ordinary shares. For a privately owned business, this is a significant dilution of ownership and potentially control, especially if directors want to make future decisions without investor influence. It is therefore less suitable where protecting control is an explicit objective.

Debt factoring could release cash quickly: if all £650,000 of receivables were eligible, the maximum advance would be £520,000. It has no share dilution and could help bridge the period before customers pay, especially as the extra order could increase working-capital needs. However, a 3% fee would cost £15,600 on a maximum advance, and the factor contacting customers could damage service relationships or make customers concerned about LoopFill’s finances. This is particularly risky when LoopFill must protect delivery performance and customer confidence with its largest customer. Factoring is also a working-capital facility, rather than an ideal permanent source for buying a long-life automated line.

LoopFill should take the £200,000 bank loan to finance the line and retain its cash buffer. This matches the five-year finance with an asset expected to support output over several years, and avoids the 18% loss of ownership. The directors should arrange factoring only as a limited contingency for selected receivables if the additional order causes a temporary cash-flow shortfall, rather than factor routinely or use it to fund the whole asset. Before committing, they should confirm that expected contribution from the new order, after training, quality-control and maintenance costs, can cover the loan’s annual debt-service commitment. This combination best protects control and immediate cash, while recognising the risk created by slow customer payments.

Northstar should use the network as a control tool rather than simply as a launch-date plan. A, C, E and F have no float, so slippage in software configuration, scanner testing or operator training delays the whole line. B and D can each move by one week without changing completion, which gives some limited scope to redeploy staff or maintenance support when production problems occur. However, that float should not be treated as spare capacity: the same maintenance technicians are required for routine production and installation, whereas the network shows dependencies but not resource constraints. If the retailer promotion can be supported by a 12-week completion, Northstar should avoid this cost and protect cash. If an 11-week completion is essential, shortening E is justified only if weekend factory access is feasible and does not disrupt output or create technician overload. A deadline shorter than 11 weeks would require action on B or D as well, because they would then be on the critical path.

NPV is calculated by discounting each forecast net cash inflow and deducting the immediate £240,000 outlay.

Year 1: £70,000 × 0.91 = £63,700
Year 2: £75,000 × 0.83 = £62,250
Year 3: £80,000 × 0.76 = £60,800
Year 4: £85,000 × 0.69 = £58,650
Year 5: £90,000 × 0.62 = £55,800

Total present value of inflows = £301,200.
NPV = £301,200 − £240,000 = £61,200.

The positive NPV supports proceeding in principle. It means that, using Northstar's required rate of return, the forecast inflows exceed the initial cost by £61,200. The line may also create benefits not fully captured by the calculation, including better serial-number traceability and fewer manual packing errors. These could protect retailer relationships and reduce costs from errors, especially when demand is growing.

However, NPV alone is not sufficient support for immediate investment. It depends on five years of forecast inflows, yet those inflows rely on retailer promotions continuing and competitors not forcing down Halo's selling price. If demand is lower than forecast, the later cash inflows and therefore the NPV will fall. NPV also measures long-term value, not Northstar's ability to pay bills in July. The £240,000 is payable immediately, despite a closing cash balance of only £96,000 and a forecast July shortfall if retailer receipts are late.

Northstar should therefore treat the positive NPV as a reason to retain the project, but proceed only alongside a credible short-term cash plan. It should improve collection of retailer receivables, release cash from surplus inventory where this does not endanger supply, and arrange suitable short-term finance if needed. It should also confirm that the line can be ready for the retailer promotion; otherwise, the assumed first-year inflow may not be achieved.

The expected seasonal contribution from continuing with Malaysia alone is:

0.70 × £780,000 + 0.30 × £270,000 = £627,000.

For dual sourcing, the expected contribution before the establishment cost is:

0.85 × £745,000 + 0.15 × £510,000 = £709,750.

After the £95,000 testing, onboarding and quality-check cost, expected contribution is £614,750. On the decision-tree figures alone, Malaysia alone is financially preferable by £12,250.

This result supports the purchasing manager's view because Malaysia has the higher expected contribution and avoids an immediate £95,000 cost when Northstar has weak cash reserves. In the normal-supply outcome, Malaysia alone produces £780,000, compared with £650,000 after allowing for the dual-source establishment cost. If the board gives greatest weight to expected financial return and cash preservation, it should retain Malaysia alone.

However, expected values can conceal a serious downside. Dual sourcing reduces the estimated probability of a serious delay from 0.30 to 0.15. In a serious-delay outcome, dual sourcing gives £415,000 after its fixed cost, compared with only £270,000 from Malaysia alone. This is important because Northstar has already experienced a port delay and nearly used all its buffer inventory. A missed retailer delivery could cause penalties and poor customer ratings, undermining the objective of growing Halo sales while protecting reliability. The UK supplier's shorter lead time and spare capacity could also make recovery from disruption quicker.

The evidence is uncertain. The probabilities come from management experience and supplier discussions, not independently verified evidence. In addition, the UK supplier has supplied only a small trial order, so its quality consistency, ability to scale and actual response during peak demand are not proven. Conversely, the Malaysian supplier's recent delay indicates that its stated normal lead time may not reflect disruption risk. Therefore, the £12,250 expected-value advantage is too narrow to be decisive.

Northstar should establish a controlled dual-source arrangement for the winter peak, subject to rapid quality validation and a confirmed allocation of volumes between suppliers. This better fits its reliability and growth objectives, despite the modest expected-contribution sacrifice. The board should fund the £95,000 only within a wider cash plan and monitor supplier performance closely; if the UK supplier fails quality or delivery testing, Northstar should not rely on it for critical peak volumes.

Northstar must distinguish clearly between profit and cash flow. It made an operating profit of £504,000, but had only £96,000 cash at the year end. Profit records revenue earned less costs incurred; it does not mean customers have paid. This distinction is particularly important because retailers usually pay 60 days after delivery while Northstar pays its main board supplier after 30 days.

Operating profit margin is £504,000 ÷ £8,400,000 × 100 = 6%. Northstar earns only £6 of operating profit per £100 of revenue. Its gross profit margin is 35%, so the business has a positive product margin, but operating expenses reduce this substantially. A 6% operating margin leaves limited protection if retailer promotions reduce selling prices, imported-board costs rise, or delays create penalties and expedited freight. Northstar should protect margin by avoiding unprofitable discounting, reducing packing errors and returns, and using the proposed line only if its cash funding and sales assumptions are secure.

The immediate priority should be cash protection. Net working capital is £1.63m, driven by £1.05m of inventory and £1.32m of receivables. The potential £382,000 July shortfall is more urgent than reported profit. Northstar should tighten credit control for retailer accounts, actively chase the potentially late receipts and agree clear payment expectations before further promotional sales. This may risk damaging retailer relationships if applied inflexibly, so it should focus first on overdue or higher-risk accounts rather than impose indiscriminate restrictions.

It should next release cash from working capital. Selling genuinely surplus slow-moving casings converts stock into cash, while reducing excessive purchasing batches should stop inventory rising further. However, it should not simply cut the board buffer to solve the cash problem: a recent port delay almost exhausted it, and a stock-out could lose sales and damage ratings. Negotiating longer supplier terms would improve cash flow but could weaken the relationship with the already critical Malaysian supplier. An overdraft is a sensible contingency for a timing mismatch, but it is finance rather than an improvement in profit and should not fund persistent excess inventory.

The packing line has a positive NPV and could improve both quality and future efficiency, so it remains a worthwhile medium-term profit action. Nevertheless, its £240,000 immediate outlay could worsen the July cash position. Northstar should prioritise receivables collection and targeted inventory release first, preserve supply resilience, and then proceed with the line only when a cash forecast shows that it can meet obligations through the promotion period. This balanced approach addresses the immediate survival risk without sacrificing the growth investment that may strengthen future profitability.

Northstar should use Lewin's three-stage model to implement the structural, job-design and technology changes as one coordinated programme. Delayering, multi-skilled cells and an automated packing line are interdependent: removing a management layer without preparing cell leaders could create uncontrolled decisions, while installing the line without trained and engaged operators could increase rather than reduce errors.

Unfreeze: Northstar first needs to create readiness for change. The managing director has announced an intended launch date, which creates urgency, but this is insufficient because supervisors fear redundancy or loss of status and assemblers fear new tasks and scanner-based measurement. Managers should explain the specific business case: demand is rising, the existing packing line may fail at peak demand, and slow functional decisions during shortages threaten retailer service. Consultation meetings should identify practical problems in proposed cells, such as skill gaps, quality escalation and staffing cover. This is not merely about gaining acceptance; production employees may identify faults in the new workflow before they affect customers.

Northstar should communicate fairly what will happen to supervisors and to the six packing employees potentially affected by automation. It should offer retraining, redeployment where feasible and transparent selection processes if redundancies cannot be avoided. Supervisors should be offered credible roles as cell coaches, quality specialists or improvement leaders rather than being treated as obstacles. It must also explain what scanning data will measure, who can see it and how it will be used. Otherwise, employees may see traceability as surveillance and resist the technology.

Change: A phased pilot is preferable to immediate compulsory implementation. Northstar could trial multi-skilled working in one production cell, with training in assembly tasks, quality checks, staffing decisions and use of the scanner. Cell leaders should have explicit authority to alter daily schedules within defined quality and spending limits, with a clear route for escalating shortages. Initial parallel quality checks and practical feedback sessions would identify whether the new responsibilities maintain product reliability.

The packing line should be installed with a detailed project plan, technician cover for normal production and a maintenance-support arrangement. Training needs to occur before handover, not after a failed launch. A fully compulsory rapid rollout may appear to protect the retailer-promotion deadline, but it risks lower morale, loss of experienced supervisors and quality failures at the point when retailer ratings matter most. Equally, an open-ended pilot is unsuitable because Northstar needs capacity for the promotion. The pilot should therefore have fixed decision points and be expanded quickly only after quality, output and employee-competence criteria are met.

Refreeze: Once the new arrangement works, Northstar should embed it through revised procedures, skills matrices, reporting lines and induction training. Performance measures should balance output with packing errors, traceability, on-time delivery, quality and safe staffing; measuring only speed through the scanning system would undermine the reliability objective. Regular reviews should resolve cross-cell inconsistencies, while recognition and development for multi-skilled employees will reinforce the new culture.

Overall, Northstar should use a firm but participative, phased implementation. It should not delay essential decisions indefinitely, but consultation, training and a controlled pilot are more likely than a compulsory launch to deliver the required capacity without damaging quality, employee commitment or retailer service.

Northstar should establish a carefully controlled dual-source arrangement, but only with active inventory and cash management. The decision is not simply whether the UK board price is higher; it is whether greater supply resilience and lower stock commitments are worth the extra costs and implementation risk during the winter peak.

Inventory control strongly supports having a UK source. At average usage, Malaysia's 10-week lead time represents 10,000 boards of demand. Adding the stated 2,000-board buffer gives an indicative 12,000-board requirement before a Malaysian delivery is received. For the UK supplier, three weeks of average demand plus the same buffer is 5,000 boards. These are planning indications rather than precise reorder levels, since maximum usage is not supplied, but they show why the Malaysian minimum order of 12,000 boards is restrictive when Northstar's stated maximum inventory is 14,000 units. A 3,000-unit UK batch gives much more scope to top up stock in smaller amounts and avoid accumulating excessive inventory.

The cash implications are significant. One Malaysian minimum order costs £220,800, whereas a UK minimum order costs £60,300. A smaller UK order therefore requires £160,500 less immediate cash. This could help Northstar reduce its £1.05m inventory and relieve pressure created by 60-day customer payment terms. However, it would be wrong to assume that lower inventory automatically solves the cash crisis. The UK board costs £1.70 more per unit, and the £95,000 onboarding, testing and quality-check cost is almost equal to Northstar's £96,000 closing cash balance. UK payment terms are also not given. Northstar needs a rolling cash forecast before paying this cost, particularly given the possible July shortfall.

Dual sourcing should improve supply-chain effectiveness because it reduces dependence on one Malaysian supplier, whose delivery was recently delayed by three weeks. The UK supplier has spare capacity and a three-week lead time, so it could provide faster replenishment or recovery when port disruption occurs. This is valuable because missed Halo deliveries may produce retailer penalties and poor online ratings. It also permits Northstar to keep some Malaysian low-cost supply while using the UK source for flexibility rather than immediately transferring all volume to the higher-cost supplier.

There are drawbacks. The UK supplier has completed only a small trial order, so quality consistency at winter volumes is uncertain. Two suppliers require specification control, incoming quality checks, forecasting discipline and clear allocation of orders. Northstar should not reduce its buffer inventory immediately after appointing the UK supplier; it should do so only after the supplier demonstrates reliable quality and delivery. Otherwise, apparent inventory savings could be followed by costly stock-outs.

The decision-tree evidence gives Malaysia alone an expected seasonal contribution of £627,000, compared with £614,750 after the dual-source setup cost. Thus, Malaysia alone has a £12,250 expected-value advantage. Yet dual sourcing halves the estimated serious-delay probability from 0.30 to 0.15 and produces a much better serious-delay contribution after setup costs. Since the estimates are based on internal experience and supplier discussions rather than independent evidence, this small expected-value difference should not outweigh Northstar's objective of protecting reliability.

Northstar should therefore qualify the UK supplier as a genuine second source before winter, subject to successful quality and capacity checks. It should retain Malaysia for stable base volumes and use the UK supplier for planned top-ups, surge demand and disruption recovery. The board should approve the £95,000 cost only alongside a cash plan that accelerates receivables and releases clearly surplus stock; otherwise, it risks solving a supply problem while creating an immediate liquidity problem.
